Orbital Temple / firmware V1.21 / brief for the twelve

Everything it can say,
everything you can say to it.

A 250 gram cube, five centimetres on a side, with thirty centimetres of steel measuring tape for an antenna. It launches on SpaceX Transporter-18 in October, circles the Earth every 96 and a half minutes, and stays up for four to ten years. Then it burns.

Everything below is real. Firmware figures are read out of the flight code and cited to the line. Orbital figures are propagated with SGP4 from a current element set. We generate all of it and hand it to you as a feed.

↓ What you can get

Nine kinds of data

Some of it the satellite measures. Most of it the ground computes.

1. What it feels

Every sixty seconds it reports its whole body at once: how much charge is left, how warm it is, whether it is in daylight, how it is turning, and how many bits a cosmic ray flipped since it last woke up. 1,440 of these a day, for years.

Onboard sensors · live frame loop.cpp:141-198

And this is the whole thing as it arrives, 120 bytes of plain text:

Every 60 s Values simulated until launch

2. Sixty seconds of its own tumbling, at thirty samples a second

On command it records 1,800 accelerometer samples over a minute and writes them to the SD card. It is the one high-rate thing on board, and the difference between it and the once-a-minute telemetry is the whole argument of the panel.

Body motion · same tumble, two instruments
/accel/rec_<millis>.bin · 21,616 bytes bytes 0-6 magic "ACCEL30" byte 7 version bytes 8-9 sample rate, uint16 LE, 30 bytes 10-11 sample count, uint16 LE, 1800 then 1800 x { float32 x, float32 y, float32 z }, LE, units of g

3. A count of the bits the cosmos flipped

Eight critical variables are held in memory three times over. Once a minute the satellite compares the copies, and where they disagree the two that match overrule the one that does not. Every repair increments a number, and that number rides in every frame.

Triple modular redundancy · one scrub cycle radiation.cpp:210-284
HoldingSEU:0
There is no radiation detector on board. The counter is a side effect of the defence, and it should rise most over the South Atlantic Anomaly. A satellite from the Global South whose bit-flip count peaks over the South Atlantic. The ground track tells you when that is.

4. Where it is, always

It has no GPS and does not need one. From the moment it is catalogued, its position, velocity, altitude and ground track are computed on the ground to the second, days ahead, by anyone.

5. Fifteen sunrises a day, each one predictable to the second

Its ascending node sits at 10:50 in the morning, so it is eclipsed on every single orbit, all year. Propagating the orbit against the Sun gives the exact instant it crosses into shadow and back out, refined by bisection down to seconds.

One orbit · 96.5 minutes, to scale SGP4 against the DE421 solar ephemeris
——
The satellite feels every one of them. Its light sensor drops at the terminator and its thermometer follows, so the rhythm is written straight into the telemetry. The exact instant comes from the ground. Put the two together and you have a sunrise it lived through, timestamped.

6. When it is over your head, and which way to point

A pass is the few minutes it is above your horizon. Over Minas Gerais that is 3.43 passes a day, 8.1 minutes each, 27.7 minutes of contact in twenty-four hours. Over your studio it is a different set of numbers, and we will compute them for wherever you are.

GET /passes?lat=40.6782&lon=-73.9442&days=7 every pass over that point: rise, peak, set, max elevation, compass bearing GET /pointing?lat=40.6782&lon=-73.9442 where it is right now, from there: azimuth, elevation, range, Doppler above the horizon, or how long until it is
You send a point. We send the trajectory from it. worked example: 40.6782, -73.9442
——
This is the same primitive that drives the Orbital Witnesses. Each of those sculptures holds a location, asks where the satellite is, and turns its pointer to face it. Anything that can make an HTTP request can do the same: a motor, a light, a speaker, a room.
One real pass · elevation and Doppler shift 468.5 MHz downlink, range rate from SGP4
——
The frequency it arrives on is its speed. Coming towards you the downlink shifts up by nearly 11 kilohertz, going away it shifts down by the same, and it crosses zero at the exact instant of closest approach. A 21.7 kilohertz glissando, ten minutes long, measured from 600 kilometres away.

7. What comes near it

The satellite is registered in SpaceX's collision-avoidance platform, which watches 23,113 objects and issues a message whenever something is predicted to pass close. Each one names the other object, the exact second of closest approach, how near it comes, and how likely a hit is.

One encounter, five messages Starlink Space Safety, conjunction data messages
——
One conjunction · what arrives Starlink Space Safety, verified live 2026-08-14
other_objectCOSMOS 2251 DEBWho. Debris and live satellites alike.
tca_utc2026-11-02T04:18:55ZWhen, to the second.
issued_utc2026-11-01T11:02:33ZWhen we were warned. The gap is a countdown.
miss_distance_m412.7How close, in metres.
relative_speed_m_s13,884How fast they pass. Nearly 14 km a second.
collision_probability3.1e-05The number itself.
miss_radial_m-38.1Passing above or below,
miss_along_track_m402.9ahead or behind,
miss_cross_track_m-84.4or off to one side.
Arrives irregularly, on its own schedule Volume unknown until it is up there
One encounter is not one message. As the tracking sharpens, the platform reissues the same event with revised numbers: a first warning thirty-six hours out, then closer estimates as the hours run down, the probability climbing and then falling away again. They share an event id, so you can pull the whole arc. That shape is free in the data.

8. The feed, which we generate and hand you

None of the ground data needs you to own an antenna. We run the propagation, pull the platform, and publish the result. It regenerates whenever the element set is updated, which after launch is roughly daily.

orbit period, altitude, inclination, node, velocity eclipse every entry and exit, to the second, with durations track sub-satellite latitude, longitude, altitude, once a minute passes for our stations or yours: rise, peak, set, elevation, bearing curve 120 samples per pass: elevation, azimuth, range, Doppler conjunctions grouped by event, with the full revision history telemetry every frame the satellite has ever sent, once it is sending
A week of it is about two megabytes, roughly a hundred times everything the satellite itself will transmit in that week. Almost everything knowable about this object is knowable without it saying a word. The few hundred bytes it does say are the only part that is a voice.

9. And the voice: a beacon that changes with how long it has been alone

Left to itself the satellite recites one of three lines of Brazilian song. Which line, and how often, depends entirely on how recently someone spoke to it. The lyric is the status field.

Three states, one hour of each
Alone, it calls every four minutes
<song line>|T+HH:MM:SS|B:<boot count>|C:YES|NO|V:<volts> Andar com fe eu vou, que a fe nao costuma faia.|T+00:01:00|B:2|C:NO|V:3.7
↑ What you can send

A work of any size, in 46 characters

401.5 MHz. Signed, small, and permanent.

10. The InterPlanetary File System, finally interplanetary

In 2014 a distributed storage protocol was given the name InterPlanetary File System. It was aspiration. Nothing about it had ever left the planet. The idea behind the name was that if you address a work by what it is rather than where it lives, the address keeps working however far apart the copies drift.

You already know the mechanism even if you have never used it directly. It is the same content-addressing that almost every artwork on a blockchain uses: the token points at a hash, and the hash is the work. What ascends here is that pointer.

A work of any size, in 46 characters
— loop.cpp:403-440
It cannot point at the wrong thing. Change one byte of the work and the address changes with it. No server to stay alive, no company to stay solvent, no domain to renew.
It fits. 46 characters, inside a single 255 byte packet, whispered at 1,256 bits per second from a cube the size of a fist.
SAT_ID-artworkAscension&@CID|ArtistName|WorkTitle#HMAC comes back as OK:ART_STORED|<CID> is kept as T+00:15:32|QmYwAPJzv5CZsnA625s3Xf2nemtYgPpHdWEz79ojWnPbdG|Artist Name|Work Title

The satellite becomes the first node of that network off the surface of the Earth. It holds addresses, it answers when asked what it holds, and it carries them until it burns. The work stays here, in your hands and in a gallery. The pointer is the part small enough to make the trip, and the part that outlives every copy.

11. How much room there is

Every command is one signed string. The envelope takes a fixed share of a 255 byte packet and what is left is yours.

Type something and watch the packet fill loop.cpp:206-268
Envelope, 68 bytes Your data, 0 bytes Free, 187 bytes

255 byte hard ceiling
SAT_ID 32 hex characters, fixed for the life of the satellite COMMAND letters and digits only, case sensitive PATH a filesystem path, unused by many commands DATA yours HMAC 16 hex characters, signed over everything before the "#"

4. Radio settings, for anyone building a receiver

SettingValueNote
Downlink frequency468.5 MHzListen here. Allow plus or minus 11 kHz for Doppler.
Uplink frequency401.5 MHzTransmitting is done by the operating stations in Brazil.
ModulationLoRaNot FSK.
Bandwidth125 kHzThe ITU filing allocates 500 kHz. The firmware uses 125.
Spreading factor9
Coding rate4/7
Sync word0x12A wrong sync word once made the satellite unreachable. It matters.
Preamble8 symbols
Packet CRCenabledLibrary default, not overridden.
Max payload255 bytesChip limit. About 187 bytes are yours.
Effective rate~1,256 bpsAbout 157 bytes a second.
Chunk size200 bytesEach piece of a file download.
TransmitterSX1276The public README says SX1262. The README is wrong.
Antenna2.2 dBiDeployable tape spring, omnidirectional, right-hand circular.
Path loss142 to 153 dBFree space, overhead to horizon.

Downlink packets carry no satellite identity, no signature and no sequence number. They are bare strings, distinguished by frequency and sync word alone, and multi-packet transfers are reassembled by arrival order.

5. Files it keeps

PathFormatWritten when
/artworks.logT+HH:MM:SS|CID|Artist|TitleEvery artworkAscension. Append only, kept until re-entry.
/names/…whatever was writtenWriteFile or AppendFile. No fixed convention.
/log.txt[<uptime ms>] <message>Every boot, every telemetry frame, hourly and daily health records.
/accel/rec_<ms>.bin16 byte header, then 1800 float32 triplesAccelRecord, and once automatically on first contact.

Directory listings cap at 100 entries, accelerometer listings at 20. Writes are refused when free space drops below one megabyte.

Where the numbers come from.
  • Firmware figures are read out of V1.21 and cited to file and line.
  • Orbital figures are propagated with SGP4 against the DE421 solar ephemeris, from a real, current element set. It is not ours yet: nothing of ours is in orbit, so the reference orbit stands in until Transporter-18 deploys and the object is catalogued, after which everything here is recomputed from ours. Expect the shape to hold and the exact times to move.
  • Passes, contact minutes and Doppler are computed for the operating station in Minas Gerais at a five degree minimum elevation. Yours on request.
  • Catalogue and conjunction figures were read live from the collision-avoidance platform on 14 August 2026.
  • Transporter-18 is projected for October 2026. SpaceX has not set a date.
